title: Credit Spreads, Default and Recovery
summary: What a spread is compensation for, the two numbers that decide whether it is enough, and the default rate at which you break even.

lesson.body:
A [[credit-spread|credit spread]] is the extra yield a borrower pays above the [[risk-free-rate|risk-free rate]] of the same maturity. It compensates the lender for four distinct things, and separating them is the whole discipline of credit analysis.

**Expected loss.** The probability of default multiplied by the loss suffered if it happens. This is the part that can be estimated.

**Unexpected loss.** Compensation for the risk that the realised outcome is worse than expected — the reason spreads exceed expected losses on average.

**Illiquidity.** Payment for holding something you may not be able to sell quickly at a fair price.

**Sentiment.** What the market currently demands for taking risk at all, which moves for reasons unrelated to any individual borrower.

**The practical consequence: a spread widening tells you nothing on its own about the borrower.** It might be a deteriorating credit, or a market repricing risk generally, and the two call for opposite responses. Comparing the borrower's spread move with its sector's separates them.

**Expected loss has exactly two inputs, and credit analysis is mostly the business of estimating them.**

**[[probability-of-default|Probability of default]]** — the chance the borrower fails to pay as promised within the period. Driven by leverage, coverage, cash flow [[volatility]] and the maturity schedule.

**[[loss-given-default|Loss given default]]** — how much you lose when it happens, expressed as a percentage. The complement of recovery: 40% recovery means 60% loss given default.

Expected loss is their product. A 3% default probability with a 60% loss rate is an expected loss of **1.8% a year**, and against a 4% spread that leaves 2.2% of net compensation.

**What determines recovery is where you sit and what secures you**, which is why [[seniority]] is not a technicality:

**Senior secured** — first claim on specific assets. Historically the highest recoveries.

**Senior unsecured** — a general claim, behind the secured lenders.

**Subordinated** — behind everyone else, and recoveries are frequently near zero.

**Equity** — last, and usually nothing.

**The same company therefore offers several different investments, and the spread differences between them are recovery differences rather than default-probability differences** — the company either fails or it does not, and everyone in the structure faces the same event.

**The most useful single calculation in credit turns a spread into a default rate you can argue about.**

A spread compensates for expected loss, so the default rate at which you break even is the spread divided by the loss given default:

At a 4% spread and a 60% loss rate, the breakeven annual default rate is 4% / 60% = **6.67%**.

That number is far more useful than the spread, because it converts a market price into a testable claim about the world. **Is 6.67% a year a plausible default rate for this kind of borrower?** For investment grade it is enormous. For a portfolio of highly levered small companies in a downturn, it is not.

Three things this reframing does immediately:

**It makes spreads comparable across seniority.** A 4% spread on senior secured debt with 80% recovery implies a 20% breakeven default rate; the same 4% on subordinated debt with 20% recovery implies 5%. Identical spread, completely different bets.

**It exposes optimistic recovery assumptions.** Everything in credit rests on the recovery estimate, and recoveries in asset-light businesses have been consistently disappointing — there is nothing to seize.

**It gives you a question rather than a number.** "This spread pays us to be wrong about defaults up to 6.67% a year" is a sentence an investment committee can actually engage with, and "the spread is 400bp" is not.
A loan pays a spread of 400bp over the risk-free rate. Estimated default probability is 3% a year and recovery in default is expected at 40%.
walkthrough: Net compensation = 400bp − 180bp = **220bp** for unexpected loss, illiquidity and sentiment.
Breakeven default rate = 4.00% / 60% = **6.67% a year**. At that rate you earn the risk-free rate and nothing more.

**Read that carefully: the spread pays you to be wrong by more than a factor of two on the default rate before you lose relative to a government bond.** That is either comfortable or not, depending entirely on whether 6.67% is plausible for this borrower type.

Now change one assumption. If recovery turns out to be 20% rather than 40%, loss given default is 80%: expected loss becomes 2.4%, net compensation 160bp, and the breakeven default rate falls to **5.00%**.
**A 20-point error in the recovery estimate consumed a quarter of the cushion.** Recovery is the assumption to interrogate, and it is the one most often taken from a historical average.

Sanity check worth reusing: **divide the spread by the loss given default and ask whether that default rate is plausible.** One division, and it converts a market quote into a claim about the world that can be argued with.

lesson.caption: The same borrower, four different investments
rows: A high breakeven default rate; the spread mostly pays for illiquidity.
A middle case, and the blend hides where the security actually sits.
A meaningful default cushion, sensitive to the [[capital-structure|capital structure]] above.
A thin cushion — the same spread is a far more aggressive bet.

lesson.body:
**Historical recoveries applied to a different structure.** Recovery data comes largely from bonds in asset-heavy businesses. A software company with no tangible assets and a large secured loan is a different proposition, and the historical average flatters it.

**Default correlation ignored.** Defaults cluster. A portfolio of a hundred loans is not a hundred independent bets — they share an economy, and the loss distribution in a downturn is far worse than an average default rate suggests.

**Ratings read as forecasts.** A rating is an opinion about relative risk, revised after the fact. It is a starting point rather than an answer, and rating transitions are themselves cyclical.

**Spread compared with the wrong risk-free rate.** A spread is only meaningful against the same maturity, and mismatched comparisons make credit look cheap or expensive for no reason.

**The extend-and-pretend problem.** An amendment that defers a maturity avoids a default without improving the borrower. Reported default rates stay low while the underlying credit quality falls, and the gap between the two is invisible in the headline statistics.

**A spread is only interpretable next to the leverage it is lending against, and the useful unit is spread per turn of leverage.**

Two loans both pay 600bp. One is senior secured at 4.0x leverage; the other is senior secured at 6.5x. The second is being paid the same to take substantially more risk — 150bp per turn against 92bp per turn.

This single ratio does most of the work in comparing [[private-credit|private credit]] vintages, because it separates the two things a headline yield conflates:

**How much you are paid**, which the market sets.

**How much risk you took to get it**, which the manager chose.

So a manager reporting stable spreads through a period when average leverage rose has, in substance, cut their price. The yield looks unchanged and the compensation per unit of risk has fallen. **This is the single most useful vintage comparison available in [[direct-lending|direct lending]], and it is not something managers volunteer.**

Ask for spread, leverage and attachment point by vintage. Three columns, and the trend across them describes underwriting discipline more honestly than any statement about it.

**Divide the spread by the loss given default and ask whether that default rate is plausible.** It turns a quote into an argument you can have.

**Ask what recovery assumption is being used, and where it came from.** Historical averages from asset-heavy issuers do not transfer to asset-light borrowers.

**Ask for spread per turn of leverage by vintage.** Stable spreads with rising leverage is a price cut in disguise.

**When a spread widens, compare it with the sector's.** Idiosyncratic widening is a credit event; sector-wide widening is a repricing of risk, and the responses differ.

**Ask how many portfolio loans have been amended or had maturities extended.** Amendments suppress reported defaults without improving credit quality, and the count is knowable.

items: A spread pays for expected loss, unexpected loss, illiquidity and sentiment — so a spread move tells you nothing about the borrower until you compare it with the sector.
Expected loss is default probability times loss given default: 3% and 60% is 1.8% a year, leaving 220bp of a 400bp spread.
Breakeven default rate is spread divided by loss given default — 6.67% here. It converts a market price into a claim about the world that can be argued with.
Recovery is the fragile assumption: moving it from 40% to 20% cut the breakeven default rate from 6.67% to 5.00%, consuming a quarter of the cushion.

questions.stem: Default probability 3% a year, recovery 40%. What is the expected annual loss, in percent?
questions.inputHint: Loss given default is one minus recovery.
questions.explanation: Against a 400bp spread this leaves 220bp for unexpected loss, illiquidity and sentiment. Splitting the spread into the part that pays for expected losses and the part that pays for everything else is the first step of any credit assessment.

questions.stem: A loan pays a 400bp spread and loss given default is 60%. What annual default rate makes you break even against the risk-free rate? Two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The value of this number is that it is arguable. "Is 6.67% a year plausible for this borrower type?" is a question a committee can debate with evidence, where "the spread is 400bp" invites no test at all.

questions.stem: Same 400bp spread, but recovery turns out to be 20% rather than 40%. What is the new breakeven default rate, in percent?
questions.explanation: A 20-point recovery error removed 167bp from the breakeven rate — a quarter of the cushion. This is why recovery assumptions deserve more scrutiny than default probabilities: they are harder to estimate and the answer is more sensitive to them.

questions.stem: Two instruments issued by the same company pay the same 400bp spread — one senior secured, one subordinated. What differs?
choices: The probability of default, which is higher for the subordinated instrument
The recovery if default happens, so the same spread implies a much lower breakeven default rate for the subordinated position
Nothing — the same issuer means the same risk
rationales: Default is a company-level event: both instruments default at the same moment. What differs is what each recovers afterwards.
Correct. Senior secured might recover 70% and subordinated 10%. The same spread therefore buys very different cushions, which makes it a far more aggressive bet at the bottom of the structure.
The issuer is the same and the claims are not, which is the entire purpose of a capital structure.
Maturities may differ and that is not what explains the recovery difference.
questions.explanation: This is why comparing spreads without seniority is meaningless, and it is also the mechanism behind capital structure arbitrage: if the market prices two claims on the same company inconsistently given their recoveries, the relative value is identifiable.

questions.stem: "We hold a hundred loans, so idiosyncratic default risk is diversified away." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — defaults cluster because borrowers share an economy, so a hundred loans are not a hundred independent bets and downturn losses far exceed an average default rate
False — diversification requires at least five hundred positions
True — a hundred positions is sufficient for diversification
False — because default correlation only matters for investment grade credit
rationales: Correct. Correlation is the whole problem: name-specific risk does diversify, and the common factor does not. In a recession the defaults arrive together, which is precisely when the portfolio can least absorb them.
There is no threshold count that solves correlation — adding names reduces idiosyncratic risk and leaves the shared exposure untouched.
Sufficient for idiosyncratic risk and irrelevant to the correlated component, which is what causes the losses that matter.
Correlation matters more in leveraged credit, not less.
questions.explanation: The right question is not how many loans there are but what they have in common: sector, size, sponsor, financing model, geography. A hundred loans to sponsor-backed mid-market software companies is one bet expressed a hundred times.

questions.stem: A direct lending manager reports stable 600bp spreads across three vintages while average portfolio leverage rose from 4.0x to 6.5x. What has happened?
choices: Nothing — the spread is unchanged, so pricing has held
Compensation per unit of risk fell from 150bp to 92bp per turn of leverage — a price cut in substance
rationales: The spread held and the risk it is being paid for grew, so the price per unit of risk fell.
Correct. 600bp over 4.0x is 150bp per turn; over 6.5x it is 92bp. The headline yield conceals a 39% reduction in compensation per turn of leverage.
Rising leverage at a constant spread is the opposite of tightening underwriting.
Recoveries generally fall as leverage rises, which makes the position worse rather than better.
questions.explanation: Spread per turn is the most useful vintage comparison in direct lending and managers rarely present it. Ask for spread, leverage and attachment point by vintage — three columns whose trend describes discipline more honestly than any assurance about it.
